title: Ranking Done Right
objective: After this lesson you will be able to choose correctly among ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK and NTILE; write deterministic top-N-per-group queries; and avoid the three classic ranking bugs (nondeterministic ties, paged RANK gaps, NTILE sizing surprises).
why: Rankings drive leaderboards, prizes, shortlists, and paginated feeds — all places where wrong ties cost money or trust. The primer named the functions; this lesson teaches their contracts: what each guarantees under ties, how NTILE distributes remainders, and why ROW_NUMBER without a unique order is a shuffling bug wearing a ranking costume.

blocks.text: **ROW_NUMBER**: 1,2,3,… — ties broken arbitrarily (which tied row gets which number is *unspecified* and can vary run to run). **RANK**: shared numbers with gaps (1,1,3 — competition '1224' style… precisely 1,2,2,4). **DENSE_RANK**: shared without gaps (1,2,2,3 — tiers). The choice is a product decision: prizes → RANK (shared prize, next skipped), tiers/labels → DENSE_RANK, stable pagination → ROW_NUMBER *with a unique tiebreaker*.

blocks.code:
-- Deterministic ranking: unique order kills tie arbitrariness (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
SELECT name, hours_studied,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC, id) AS rn,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS rnk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS dense_rnk
FROM developers
ORDER BY hours_studied DESC, id;
blocks.caption: The id tiebreaker makes ROW_NUMBER stable; RANK/DENSE_RANK need none

blocks.text: The `, id` tiebreaker is the whole lesson in one clause: ROW_NUMBER over non-unique ordering is nondeterministic — same query, different runs, different numbers for tied rows. Any downstream use (pagination, shortlists, dedup by rn = 1) inherits the instability. Unique total order or it isn't a ranking, it's a shuffle.

**`NTILE(n)`** splits ordered rows into n near-equal buckets: sizes differ by at most one, with **earlier buckets getting the extra rows**. 14 developers into 4 quartiles → 4,4,3,3 (buckets 1–2 hold 4). The remainder rule matters whenever you label 'top quartile' — NTILE(4) = 1 is the top ~quarter, and bucket boundaries shift as data grows, so persist labels, never recompute-and-compare across time naively.

blocks.code:
-- Quartile buckets + top-quartile shortlist (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
SELECT name, hours_studied,
  NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS quartile
FROM developers;
-- Shortlist: wrap and filter quartile = 1 (rank-inside/filter-outside, Ch.1 pipeline).
blocks.caption: NTILE buckets: earlier buckets absorb remainders

blocks.text: Combine partitioning with ranking: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY role ORDER BY hours_studied DESC, id)` then `WHERE rn <= N` outside. Three production details: partition by the grouping dimension, order deterministically *within* partitions (tiebreaker!), and remember ties policy — top-2 with RANK can return 3+ rows on ties (sometimes desired for prizes, disastrous for fixed-size feeds).

blocks.title: RANK in fixed-size slots
blocks.text: Leaderboard showing exactly 10 rows must use ROW_NUMBER (exactly 10 numbers exist) — RANK with ties returns 9 or 12 unpredictably. Conversely, prize tiers must use RANK/DENSE_RANK (ties share honestly). Mismatching function to slot is the classic leaderboard bug.

blocks.query: SELECT role, COUNT(*) AS devs FROM developers GROUP BY role ORDER BY devs DESC;
blocks.note: Run this partition inventory in the sandbox — 4 roles, their sizes. Every top-N-per-group query below operates inside these partitions: know the group sizes before ranking within them (a group of 2 makes 'top 3' meaningless).

items: ROW_NUMBER: arbitrary tie-breaks (add unique order) · RANK: shared with gaps · DENSE_RANK: shared tiers
NTILE(n): near-equal buckets, earlier buckets take remainders — persist labels, don't compare across time naively
Top-N per group: partition + deterministic order + outer filter; RANK can overfill fixed slots
Tiebreaker (`, id`) converts shuffles into rankings

exercise.prompt: (a) In the sandbox, run the partition inventory and note the smallest role group. (b) In real SQLite/PostgreSQL, write: (i) deterministic ROW_NUMBER leaderboard with tiebreaker; (ii) top-2 per role; (iii) quartile buckets with a top-quartile shortlist. (c) State which function serves a 10-row fixed feed vs a shared-prize contest, with the one-line reason each.
hints: Leaderboard: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC, id). Top-2-per-role: PARTITION BY role, same deterministic order, outer WHERE rn <= 2.
Quartiles: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC), outer filter = 1. Check bucket sizes sum to 14 (4+4+3+3).
Fixed feed → ROW_NUMBER (exactly N numbers exist). Shared prizes → RANK (ties share honestly, gaps reflect it).
exercise.solution:
-- (b-i) deterministic leaderboard (real SQLite / PostgreSQL)
SELECT name, hours_studied,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC, id) AS rn
FROM developers ORDER BY rn;
-- (b-ii) top-2 per role
SELECT role, name FROM (
  SELECT role, name,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY role ORDER BY hours_studied DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM developers) WHERE rn <= 2;
-- (b-iii) quartiles + shortlist
SELECT name FROM (
  SELECT name, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS q FROM developers)
WHERE q = 1;
-- (c) fixed feed: ROW_NUMBER (exact cardinality); prizes: RANK (honest ties).
exercise.why: Three ranking jobs, three correct functions, one discipline (deterministic order where cardinality matters). The exercise makes function choice a product decision, not a habit.

quiz.q: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) with tied hours returns different numbers across runs. Why, and fix?
options: Ties break arbitrarily without a unique order — add a tiebreaker (e.g. , id) for a deterministic total order
quiz.explain: Non-unique ordering leaves tie assignment unspecified. Unique tiebreakers convert shuffles into stable rankings — mandatory for pagination and shortlists.

quiz.q: 14 rows, NTILE(4) ORDER BY x DESC. Bucket sizes?
options: 4,4,3,3 — sizes differ by ≤1, earlier buckets take remainders
quiz.explain: Remainder rule: 14 = 3×4 + 2, so the first two buckets hold 4. Persist quartile labels; recomputation shifts boundaries as data grows.

quiz.q: Fixed 10-row leaderboard uses RANK and sometimes shows 9 or 12 rows. Fix?
options: Switch to ROW_NUMBER with deterministic order — exactly 10 numbers always exist; RANK shares numbers on ties
quiz.explain: Cardinality contracts differ: ROW_NUMBER guarantees N rows for top-N; RANK guarantees honest ties. Slot type dictates function.

quiz.q: Top-2-per-role with RANK returns 3 developers for a role. Bug or correct?
options: Correct if 2nd place ties: RANK shares honestly, overfilling fixed expectations — decide intended policy explicitly
quiz.explain: RANK's honesty overfills fixed slots. For prizes this is correct (shared 2nd); for feeds switch to ROW_NUMBER. Policy first, function second.

summary: Rank by contract: ROW_NUMBER (+tiebreaker) for exact cardinalities, RANK for honest prizes, DENSE_RANK for tiers, NTILE for quantile buckets with known remainder rules. Top-N per group partitions deterministically and filters outside.
next: Ranked rows stand alone — now relate them to neighbors: previous/next comparisons, deltas, and running state with LAG/LEAD. Next: navigation functions.
